story: In October 1851, astronomer William Lassell discovered Ariel, an extraordinary moon orbiting Uranus. Composed of nearly equal parts water ice and rock, Ariel is the brightest of Uranus's major moons and is tidally locked, keeping one face perpetually turned toward its host planet every two and a half days. When NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft executed the only close flyby of Ariel in January 1986, it revealed a surprisingly dynamic world. Unlike its heavily cratered neighbors, Ariel features the youngest surface among Uranus's major satellites. The moon is scarred by dramatic fault-bounded valleys called grabens and smooth plains formed by extrusive cryovolcanism—where molten ice and liquid water erupted across the frozen crust. Spectroscopic data confirmed carbon dioxide on its surface, and modern modeling suggests Ariel may harbor a secret subsurface ocean beneath its icy shell, keeping this distant moon active far longer than expected.
angle: Ariel is Uranus's brightest moon, carved by ancient ice-volcanoes and potentially hiding a liquid ocean beneath its frozen crust.

claims.claim: William Lassell discovered Ariel on October 24, 1851.
Ariel was named by John Herschel at the request of William Lassell.
Ariel's name comes from characters in Shakespeare's The Tempest and Alexander Pope's The Rape of the Lock.
Ariel is composed of roughly equal parts water ice and rocky silicate material.
Carbon dioxide has been detected on Ariel's surface.
Ariel is tidally locked, keeping the same face pointing toward Uranus as it orbits.
Ariel completes an orbit around Uranus in about 2 to 2.5 Earth days.
Ariel has the brightest and most reflective surface of Uranus's major moons.
Ariel has the youngest surface and showed the most recent geologic activity among Uranus's large moons.
Ariel's surface is transected by grabens, which are fault-bounded valleys and canyons.
Ariel may host a subsurface liquid ocean beneath its icy crust.
Ariel was visited up close only once, by NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft in January 1986.
Ariel's smooth plains suggest past cryovolcanism where liquid water or molten ice flowed onto the surface.

disputed: Whether John Herschel or William Lassell originally devised the names of Uranus's moons (attribute: according to historical accounts, Herschel suggested the names at Lassell's request).
The exact depth and current state of Ariel's subsurface ocean (attribute: past thermal models suggested it froze long ago, while recent studies model an active ocean tens of kilometers deep).
